name: DMM Director Auto-Locking Carabiner
title: DMM Director Carabiner: Auto-Locking Arborist Biner
meta: The DMM Director carabiner is an auto-locking biner for arborist climbing and rigging systems. What it does on the saddle, how to check it, and typical price.
tagline: A DMM auto-locking carabiner for climbers who want a dependable gate on every clip.
summary: The DMM Director carabiner is an auto-locking connector from DMM, the Welsh hardware maker many tree climbers already trust for rings, swivels and biners. It is a solid choice for linking a hitch climber, a rope wrench tether or a lanyard to the saddle bridge.
highlights: Auto-locking gate that closes and locks on its own
Made by DMM, a long-standing climbing hardware maker
Suits bridge, lanyard and hitch-climber connections
Smooth gate action that works with gloves on
Check the markings on the spine for rated strength

body.h: Where the Director fits in a climbing system
p: Most climbers carry a handful of auto-locking carabiners and assign each one a job. The Director is the kind of biner you put on the bridge to hold a hitch climber, on the end of a lanyard, or on a rope wrench tether. An auto-locking gate means you do not have to remember to spin a sleeve closed every time you reclip, which matters when you are moving through the canopy all day.

Before you build it into your kit, check that the gate opening and basket fit the hardware it will live on, and that it sits loaded along the spine rather than across the gate. Compare it with other auto-locking carabiners if you need a different shape or gate style.

A good habit is to dedicate the Director to one position in your system and leave it there, so you always know its history. Mixing life-support biners with the ones you use to hang a handsaw or a water bottle makes it hard to track which carabiner took a fall or got dropped on the driveway. Mark it with tape or a color code if your kit has several look-alike biners.

Read the strength ratings stamped on the spine and gate, and make sure they meet the requirement for how you plan to use the biner. Look for grooves worn by rope, sharp edges, cracks, and a gate that sticks, fails to close fully, or does not lock on its own. Retire any carabiner that has taken a hard drop onto a hard surface or shows damage.
Life-support gear must meet the applicable standard, be used per the manufacturer's instructions and ANSI Z133, be inspected before every climb, and be used only by trained climbers.

faq.q: Is the DMM Director good for tree climbing?
faq.a: Yes, as long as its markings meet the standard you work to and it fits the hardware you connect it to. Auto-locking gates are the norm for climbing connections in tree work.

faq.q: How do I know the strength rating?
faq.a: Read the ratings stamped on the carabiner itself and the DMM instructions that come with it. Do not rely on a listing alone.

name: The Tree Climber's Guide, 4th Edition
title: The Tree Climber's Guide 4th Edition (ISA)
meta: The Tree Climber's Guide 4th edition from ISA covers gear, knots, climbing systems and safe work practice. Who it suits, what's inside, and typical price.
tagline: ISA's core study text for tree climbers, from first knots to modern climbing systems.
summary: The Tree Climber's Guide 4th edition is the International Society of Arboriculture's study book for tree climbers, covering equipment, knots, climbing techniques and safe work practice. It is a standard reference for new climbers and for anyone preparing for the ISA Certified Tree Worker climber specialist credential.
highlights: Published by the International Society of Arboriculture
Covers climbing gear, knots and climbing systems
Includes work positioning, pruning and safety practice
Common study text for ISA tree worker credentials
Useful for training new climbers on a crew
specs: Tree climbing and safe work practice

p: This is a working climber's textbook. It walks through the gear that makes up a climbing system, the knots and hitches tree workers rely on, ways of getting into the tree, moving through the canopy, and positioning to work. It also covers safety on the job site, including aerial rescue, tool handling aloft and crew communication.

The fourth edition brings the content in line with how climbers work now, including the move toward single rope systems and mechanical devices alongside traditional moving rope techniques. Expect clear illustrations and plain explanations rather than a hard sell on any one method.

Crew leaders often use it as the backbone of a training plan: assign a chapter, then walk through the same knots, gear checks and climbing set-ups on the ground at the shop. Having one shared reference keeps the whole crew using the same terms for gear and commands, which matters when people are talking between the canopy and the ground.

New climbers get the most out of it, but it also earns a place in the truck for crew leaders who train people. It pairs well with hands-on instruction; no book replaces a qualified trainer and time in the tree. Browse other arborist books and training materials if you are building a study shelf.
If you are preparing for an ISA credential, check the current exam requirements with ISA so you study from the edition they reference.

faq.q: Is the 4th edition the one used for ISA exams?
faq.a: It is ISA's current climber study text as of this listing, but check ISA's exam information before you study, since references can change.

faq.q: Is this book enough to learn to climb?
faq.a: No. It is a strong reference, but climbing must be learned with a qualified trainer and practiced under supervision.

name: Husqvarna Battery-Powered Ascender (Tool Only)
title: Husqvarna Battery Powered Ascender, Tool Only
h1: Husqvarna Battery-Powered Ascender, Without Battery or Charger
meta: The Husqvarna battery powered ascender, sold without battery or charger, takes the work out of long ascents on rope. How it fits a climb and what to check.
tagline: A motorized rope ascender for long or repeated climbs. Battery sold separately.
summary: The Husqvarna battery powered ascender is a motorized rope ascender that hauls the climber up the line so energy goes into the work instead of the climb. This listing is the tool only, without a battery or charger, for crews already running compatible Husqvarna batteries.
highlights: Motorized ascent on a fixed rope
Sold without battery or charger
Cuts fatigue on tall trees and repeated ascents
Fits crews already on Husqvarna battery tools
Requires training and a backup system per the manual
specs: Ascender only; battery and charger sold separately

body.h: Why crews use a powered ascender
p: On a big removal or a day of tall pruning, the climb up is often the hardest part. A powered ascender takes over that work on a fixed line, so the climber reaches the tie-in point fresher and can make repeat ascents without burning out. It also helps on long access climbs where a mechanical ascent system would take several minutes of hard effort.

Buying the tool only makes sense if you already run compatible Husqvarna batteries. Confirm which batteries and chargers Husqvarna lists for this ascender before ordering, since runtime and fit depend on the pack.

Think about how the crew will run it day to day. Keep batteries charged and rotated, decide who carries the ascender between trees, and build a pre-climb check into the routine just as you would for a saddle or a rope. A powered unit adds weight on the saddle, so plan where it rides once you reach the work and switch to your working system.

A powered ascender is life-support equipment and changes how a climbing system is rigged. Follow the Husqvarna manual for anchor, rope type and diameter, backup and descent, and get hands-on training before using it in a tree. Compare manual options in ascent and descent gear if you climb only occasionally.
Life-support gear must meet the applicable standard, be used per the manufacturer's instructions and ANSI Z133, be inspected before every climb, and be used only by trained climbers.

faq.q: Does this ascender include a battery?
faq.a: No. This listing is the ascender only. Buy a compatible Husqvarna battery and charger separately, as listed in the manual.

faq.q: Can I use any rope with it?
faq.a: No. Use only the rope types and diameters the manufacturer specifies, and set up the anchor and backup exactly as the manual describes.

name: CAMP Turbo Knee Ascent System
title: CAMP Turbo Knee Ascent System for SRS Climbing
meta: The CAMP Turbo Knee is a knee ascender system that helps you walk up a single rope with less effort. How it works on SRS ascents, setup tips, and price.
tagline: A knee-mounted ascent system for single rope climbers who want a smoother rope walk.
summary: The CAMP Turbo Knee is a knee ascender system that lets a climber walk up a single rope, with the knee and foot sharing the work so the arms stay fresh. It suits arborists who make regular SRS ascents and want a more efficient climb than footlocking or hip thrusting.
highlights: Knee-mounted ascent for single rope climbing
Lets legs do most of the work on the way up
Pairs with a foot ascender for a rope-walking setup
Adjustable to fit the climber
Made by CAMP, an Italian climbing hardware maker

body.h: How a knee ascender changes the climb
p: A knee ascender keeps a rope clamp riding at your knee, so each step pushes the clamp up and the rope feeds through your chest or saddle device. Combined with a foot ascender on the other leg, it turns the ascent into a steady walk up the line. Most climbers find they arrive at the tie-in with more left in their arms and grip.

It takes some tuning. Spend time on the ground adjusting strap lengths so the clamp sits where it should, and make sure the rope runs cleanly without the system twisting your leg. A tail weight or rope tender helps the rope feed on the first few steps.

Climbers coming from footlocking or a hip-thrust ascent usually need a few sessions to find a rhythm. Start on a low limb or a practice rope, keep the steps short, and focus on standing straight up rather than pulling with the arms. Once the straps are set, it goes on and comes off quickly enough to use on every tree that needs a long rope ascent.

body.h: Fit with the rest of your kit
p: The Turbo Knee is an ascent aid, not the device that holds you. Your primary climbing system still has to be rigged and backed up correctly. Browse other foot ascenders and foot loops to round out a rope-walking setup.
Life-support gear must meet the applicable standard, be used per the manufacturer's instructions and ANSI Z133, be inspected before every climb, and be used only by trained climbers.

faq.q: Do I need a foot ascender too?
faq.a: Most climbers pair a knee ascender with a foot ascender on the opposite leg for a full rope-walking system. Follow CAMP's instructions for compatible setups.

faq.q: Can the Turbo Knee be my only attachment to the rope?
faq.a: No. It is an ascent aid. Your primary life-support device must be connected and backed up per the manufacturer's instructions.

name: Husqvarna Rope Storage Bag
title: Husqvarna Rope Bag for Climbing and Rigging Line
meta: The Husqvarna rope bag keeps climbing or rigging line clean, flaked and ready to deploy at the base of the tree. What to look for in a rope bag and price.
tagline: A rope storage bag from Husqvarna for keeping line clean and tangle-free between jobs.
summary: The Husqvarna rope bag is a storage bag for climbing line or rigging rope that keeps it out of the dirt and flaked so it deploys without knots. It is a simple way to make rope last longer and make set-up faster on every job.
highlights: Keeps rope clean between jobs
Flaked rope deploys without tangles
Easy to carry from truck to tree
Husqvarna branding to match your saw kit
Useful for climbing line or rigging rope
specs: Climbing line or rigging rope storage

body.h: Why a rope bag pays for itself
p: Grit is what wears rope out. Sawdust, sand and mud work into the braid and cut fibers from the inside every time the rope runs through a device or over a branch. A rope bag keeps line off the ground at the base of the tree and keeps it out of the truck bed between jobs.

A bag also speeds up set-up. Flake the rope in from the end at the close of the day and it pays back out cleanly the next morning, instead of coming out of a pile as a knot. Many climbers keep one bag per rope so the climbing line and rigging line never mix.

If you run more than one rope, label the bags or pick different colors so the climbing line never ends up in the rigging pile. Mixed-up rope is a real problem on busy jobs, since a climbing line that has been used to lower wood should be retired from life support. Keeping each rope in its own bag makes that separation simple.

body.h: Using and caring for the bag
p: Check that the bag is big enough for the rope you plan to store; a long length of thick rigging line needs much more room than a climbing line. Compare sizes in rope bags if you need a larger option.
Empty the bag now and then and shake out debris. Store rope dry and out of sunlight, and inspect the line itself before every climb rather than trusting that a bagged rope is a sound rope.

faq.q: Can I store a wet rope in the bag?
faq.a: Let rope dry out before long-term storage. Storing it wet can lead to mildew and makes inspection harder.

faq.q: Will it fit a rigging rope?
faq.a: It depends on the rope's diameter and length. Check the bag's capacity against your rope before you buy.

name: Freeworker TreeAustria 3.2 Climbing Harness
title: TreeAustria 3.2 Climbing Harness: European Saddle
meta: The TreeAustria 3.2 harness is a European-style arborist climbing saddle with a sliding bridge. How it climbs, who it fits, what to check, and typical price.
tagline: A European-style bridge harness for climbers who move a lot in the tree.
summary: The TreeAustria 3.2 harness is a European-style arborist climbing saddle built around a bridge attachment, made for climbers who spend long days working and moving through the canopy. It is a popular choice for climbers who want free movement at the waist and a comfortable sit.
highlights: European-style arborist climbing saddle
Bridge attachment for free movement at the waist
Built for long days aloft
Fits modern SRS and MRS climbing systems
Inspect bridge and webbing before every climb

p: European saddles like the TreeAustria put the main attachment on a bridge, so the climbing system can slide side to side as you turn, reach and work. That makes it easy to face the work without fighting the tie-in point. Climbers coming from older saddles with fixed D-rings usually notice the freedom of movement first.

Fit matters more than any feature list. Try the harness on and hang in it if you can, check leg loop and waist adjustment, and set up gear loops and side D-rings so your lanyard and saw sit where you want them.

Think about the attachments you use every day before you buy. Side D-rings carry the lanyard, the rear or side loops carry the saw, and the bridge carries the main system and often a hitch climber or rope wrench. A saddle that puts each of those where your hands expect them saves a lot of fumbling over a full day of climbing and cutting.

The bridge is a wear item. Check it for abrasion, glazing and cut fibers before every climb and replace it on the schedule in the manual. Inspect stitching, buckles and webbing too. Compare other European saddles if you want a different fit.
Life-support gear must meet the applicable standard, be used per the manufacturer's instructions and ANSI Z133, be inspected before every climb, and be used only by trained climbers.

faq.q: Can I use the TreeAustria 3.2 for SRS?
faq.a: Yes. Bridge saddles are widely used for both SRS and MRS. Follow the manufacturer's instructions for attachment points and bridge setup.

faq.q: How often should the bridge be replaced?
faq.a: Follow the manufacturer's guidance and replace it sooner if inspection shows wear, cuts, glazing or contamination.

name: ISC Apex Rope Wrench
title: ISC Apex Rope Wrench for SRS Tree Climbing
meta: The ISC Apex rope wrench adds friction above your hitch so you can climb and descend smoothly on a single rope system. How it works, setup notes, and price.
tagline: A rope wrench for SRS climbers who want a hitch that tends and descends smoothly.
summary: The ISC Apex rope wrench is a friction device for single rope technique that sits above your friction hitch, adding friction and steering the rope so the hitch runs smoothly. It lets climbers use a familiar hitch on a stationary rope system with controlled descents.
highlights: Adds friction above a friction hitch on SRS
Lets you use a familiar hitch on a stationary rope
Smooth, controllable descents
Works with a tether to the hitch or bridge
From ISC, a UK hardware maker

p: On a single rope, a friction hitch alone can grab and chatter, especially on descent. A rope wrench sits above the hitch and runs the rope through a curved path, adding just enough friction that the hitch can do its job smoothly. The result is a system that climbs, works and descends a lot like the moving rope setups many climbers learned on.
The wrench connects to the hitch by a short tether, and that tether length affects how the system tends. Set it up per ISC's instructions and test it close to the ground before climbing.

Many climbers find the wrench makes it easy to move from moving rope to stationary rope work without relearning everything. You keep a hitch you already trust, gain the efficiency of climbing on a fixed line, and can still work out on limbs with good control. Expect to spend some time adjusting hitch wraps and tether length until the system feels right.
Rope diameter and construction change how much friction you get, so match the wrench and hitch cord to your climbing line. Compare it with other SRS devices if you want a fully mechanical option.

Inspect the wrench for grooves, sharp edges and cracks, and replace worn parts as the manual directs. Life-support gear must meet the applicable standard, be used per the manufacturer's instructions and ANSI Z133, be inspected before every climb, and be used only by trained climbers.

faq.q: Do I still need a friction hitch with the Apex?
faq.a: Yes. A rope wrench works with a friction hitch below it. Follow ISC's instructions for hitch, tether and rope compatibility.

faq.q: Can the Apex be used for moving rope climbing?
faq.a: It is designed for single rope technique. Use it only in the configurations the manufacturer describes.

name: Yale Black Beeline 10mm Hitch Cord, by the Foot
title: Yale Black Beeline 10mm Hitch Cord by the Foot
h1: Yale Black Beeline 10mm, by the Foot
meta: Yale Black Beeline 10mm hitch cord sold by the foot, for tying your own split tails, eye-to-eyes and prusiks. How to pick a length, care tips, and price.
tagline: Yale's 10mm Beeline hitch cord in black, cut to the length you need.
summary: Yale Black Beeline 10mm is a friction hitch cord sold by the foot, so you can cut exactly the length you need for split tails, prusiks and other hitches. It is the same Beeline cord Yale uses in its finished hitch cords, in a black color that is easy to tell apart from your climbing line.
highlights: 10mm Beeline hitch cord from Yale Cordage
Sold by the foot so you choose the length
Black color stands out against most climbing lines
For tied split tails, prusiks and friction hitches
Heat-resistant cover suits friction hitch use

body.h: Why buy hitch cord by the foot
p: Climbers tie different hitches with different lengths of cord, and the right length depends on the hitch, your climbing line and how many wraps you use. Buying by the foot lets you cut a split tail that fits your Distel or VT, or tie spare prusiks for the gear bag, without paying for sewn terminations you do not need.
A 10mm cord gives a bit more bite and durability than an 8mm, and pairs with many 11.5 to 13mm climbing lines. Test any new hitch on the ground and adjust wraps before climbing on it.

Keep track of how much cord each hitch takes once you settle on a setup, so you can cut replacements to the same length every time. Many climbers also keep a spare length of the same cord in the gear bag, so a worn split tail can be swapped out on the job instead of climbing on a tired one until the end of the day.

Tied terminations must be dressed and set correctly and checked every time you climb. Heat and wear take their toll on hitch cord faster than on rope, so inspect for glazing, flat spots and cover damage and retire it early. Finished split tails and eye-to-eyes are in tech cordage.
Life-support gear must meet the applicable standard, be used per the manufacturer's instructions and ANSI Z133, be inspected before every climb, and be used only by trained climbers.

faq.q: How much Beeline do I need for a split tail?
faq.a: It depends on the hitch and your rope. Many climbers start around 30 to 36 inches for a split tail and adjust after testing on the ground.

faq.q: Will 10mm Beeline work on my climbing line?
faq.a: It suits many common arborist climbing lines, but test the hitch with your exact rope before trusting it aloft.

name: Husqvarna Starter Assembly for T540XP Mark III
keyword: husqvarna t540xp mark iii starter assembly
title: Husqvarna T540XP Mark III Starter Assembly
h1: Husqvarna Starter Assembly for T540XP Mark III Chainsaw
meta: Replacement Husqvarna starter assembly for the T540XP Mark III top-handle chainsaw. When to replace it, how to confirm fit, and the typical street price.
tagline: A replacement recoil starter assembly for the Husqvarna T540XP Mark III top-handle saw.
summary: This Husqvarna T540XP Mark III starter assembly is a replacement recoil starter for the climbing saw many tree crews rely on. It is the fix when the pull cord will not recoil, the housing is cracked, or the pawls no longer catch.
highlights: Replacement starter assembly for the T540XP Mark III
Fixes broken recoil, cracked housing or slipping start
Gets a key climbing saw back in the rope bag
Confirm fit by model and serial number
Simple swap for a competent saw mechanic

p: Top-handle saws live hard lives: they get dropped, banged against stems and started dozens of times a day. Common starter problems are a cord that will not rewind, a recoil spring that has let go, a cracked housing, or a starter that spins without catching the flywheel. Replacing the full assembly is often faster than rebuilding the old one on the tailgate.
Check your saw's model and serial number against the parts listing before ordering. Mark III saws use parts that may differ from earlier T540XP versions.

On a busy crew a starter failure usually happens at the worst time, with a climber already tied in and waiting for the saw. Many shops keep a spare starter assembly for each model of top-handle saw on the trucks, so a broken recoil means a ten-minute swap on the tailgate instead of a lost morning and a trip to the dealer.

Swapping a starter is a straightforward job, but follow Husqvarna's service information and use the right fasteners. Make sure the saw is cool and the spark plug lead is disconnected before you work on it. More replacement parts are in power equipment parts.
Top-handle saws are specialized tools for trained climbers working aloft. Use them as Husqvarna and ANSI Z133 direct.

faq.q: Will this starter fit an older T540XP?
faq.a: Not necessarily. Confirm compatibility for your exact model and version before ordering.

faq.q: Can I replace just the cord?
faq.a: If only the cord is worn, you can usually restring it. Replace the assembly when the housing, spring or pawls are damaged.

name: All Gear Branch Saver Synthetic Cable System
title: All Gear Branch Saver Synthetic Cable System
h1: All Gear Branch Saver Synthetic Cable System
meta: The All Gear Branch Saver is a synthetic cable system for supporting weak limbs and codominant stems. How synthetic cabling works, install notes, and price.
tagline: A synthetic tree cabling system for supplemental support of limbs and codominant stems.
summary: The All Gear Branch Saver is a synthetic cable system for supplemental support of weak limbs and codominant stems, an alternative to steel cable for many cabling jobs. It is aimed at arborists who want a lighter, faster install that works with the tree's natural movement.
highlights: Synthetic cabling for supplemental tree support
Lighter and quicker to install than steel
Allows some natural movement in the canopy
No drilling for many installs
Inspect regularly after installation
specs: Supplemental support of limbs and stems

p: Cabling limits how far a weak union or heavy limb can move in a storm. Synthetic systems like the Branch Saver wrap the stems instead of relying only on drilled hardware, are light enough to carry up in a single trip, and let the tree sway rather than holding it rigid. Many arborists reach for synthetic systems on small to medium cabling jobs and on trees where drilling is not desirable.

Choosing the right system and install location is an assessment call. The general practice is to place cables well up from the weak union, but follow the manufacturer's instructions and ANSI A300 guidance for the specific tree.

Synthetic systems also suit work where weight and access matter. A climber can carry the whole kit up in one trip, install it without heavy tools, and adjust it in place. That makes it practical on large trees with several stems to support, where hauling steel cable, drills and hardware would add a lot of time and effort to the job.

Size the system to the stems you are supporting and follow All Gear's instructions for set-up and tension. Schedule regular inspections, since synthetic cable can be damaged by abrasion, UV and wildlife. Related hardware and rope are in rigging rope.
Cabling is supplemental support, not a guarantee that a limb will not fail. Work aloft only with trained crew, following ANSI Z133.

faq.q: Does synthetic cabling require drilling?
faq.a: Many synthetic systems wrap around stems and need no drilling. Follow the manufacturer's instructions for the specific system.

faq.q: How often should it be inspected?
faq.a: Follow the manufacturer's recommendation and inspect after major storms. Check for abrasion, UV damage and correct position.

name: Husqvarna 550XP Mark II Hand Guard
title: Husqvarna 550XP Mark II Hand Guard (Chain Brake)
meta: Replacement front hand guard for the Husqvarna 550XP Mark II chainsaw, which also works the chain brake. When to replace it, fit checks, and typical price.
tagline: Replacement front hand guard and chain brake lever for the 550XP Mark II.
summary: This Husqvarna 550XP Mark II hand guard is the replacement front guard that protects your left hand and activates the chain brake. If yours is cracked, loose or no longer trips the brake reliably, replace it before the saw goes back to work.
highlights: Front hand guard for the 550XP Mark II
Also serves as the chain brake lever
Replace if cracked, loose or not tripping the brake
Confirm fit by model before ordering
Keeps a key safety feature working
specs: Front hand guard / chain brake lever

p: On the 550XP Mark II, the front hand guard does two jobs. It shields your left hand from branches and a thrown chain, and it is the lever that applies the chain brake, by hand or by inertia in a kickback. A cracked or sloppy guard can fail to trigger the brake when you need it most.

Felling, limbing and bucking all put this guard close to brush and stems, so it takes knocks. Check it at the start of each day: it should snap firmly into the on and off positions and the brake should stop the chain at speed.

Small cracks often start around the pivot and mounting points, so look there first when the saw is clean. A guard that has been patched with tape or zip ties is a sign it is time to replace it. Keep the chain brake mechanism clean of sawdust and pitch too, since buildup can slow the brake even with a new guard fitted.

Follow Husqvarna's service information when swapping the guard, and test the chain brake before cutting. If the brake band or spring is also worn, replace those too. Other replacement parts are in power equipment parts.
Never run a saw with a damaged or missing chain brake. Wear chainsaw protective gear and follow ANSI Z133 and the operator's manual.

faq.q: Does the hand guard include the brake band?
faq.a: Usually not. The guard is the lever. Check the brake band and spring separately and replace them if worn.

faq.q: Will it fit the original 550XP?
faq.a: Confirm fit for your exact model. Mark II parts may differ from the earlier 550XP.

name: Omni-Block 2.6 with Loopie Sling
title: Omni-Block 2.6 with Loopie Sling: Rigging Kit
meta: The Rock Exotica Omni-Block 2.6 paired with a loopie sling makes a quick, adjustable rigging point for light to mid-size wood. How it rigs and typical price.
tagline: Swiveling Omni-Block 2.6 pulley with an adjustable loopie sling for quick rigging points.
summary: The Omni-Block 2.6 with loopie sling pairs Rock Exotica's swiveling 2.6 in pulley with an adjustable loopie, so you can set a rigging point on almost any stem in seconds. It is a favorite for light rigging, speedlines and redirects.
highlights: Rock Exotica Omni-Block 2.6 swiveling pulley
Paired with an adjustable loopie sling
Side plates open to load mid-line
Swivel lets the block align with the load
Good for light rigging, redirects and speedlines

body.h: Why the Omni-Block and loopie work together
p: The Omni-Block's side plates open so you can drop the lowering line in mid-rope, and its swivel lets the pulley turn to face the load. A loopie sling cinches around the stem and adjusts to the diameter, so one sling covers a wide range of rigging points. Together they make a fast, compact rigging kit that rides on the saddle without much weight.
This combination is aimed at lighter rigging: brush, small tops and limb work, plus redirects and speedline anchors. For big wood, step up to a dedicated rigging block and heavier sling.

The kit rides light on the saddle, so a climber can carry it up and set a rigging point exactly where it is needed rather than relying on a natural crotch. That gives more control over where pieces swing and land, protects the bark at the rigging point, and keeps friction predictable for the ground worker running the lowering line from the base.

Check the strength markings on the pulley and the sling's rating, and make sure the whole system, including rope and connectors, is matched to the forces involved. Rigging loads are dynamic and can be far higher than the weight of the piece. Compare options in adjustable slings.

Inspect the sheave, axle, swivel and side plates for wear and the sling for cuts or glazing before each job. Rig within the rated strength of every component, inspect gear before each job, and make sure the crew is trained in rigging practice under ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions.

faq.q: Can I use this kit for climbing?
faq.a: Use any component for life support only if it is rated and marked for that use and the manufacturer allows it. This kit is sold for rigging.

faq.q: What rope works through the Omni-Block 2.6?
faq.a: Check Rock Exotica's markings and instructions for the maximum rope diameter before rigging.

name: ArbPro Laces for Clip N Step and Evo Boots
title: ArbPro Laces for Clip N Step and Evo Boots
h1: ArbPro Laces for Clip N Step and Evo Boots
meta: Replacement ArbPro boot laces made for the Clip N Step and Evo arborist boots. Why worn laces matter on spurs and in the tree, plus fit tips and typical price.
tagline: Replacement laces for ArbPro Clip N Step and Evo climbing boots.
summary: These ArbPro boot laces are replacements made for the Clip N Step and Evo arborist boots. A fresh set keeps your boots snug on spurs and in the canopy, where a loose or snapped lace is more than a nuisance.
highlights: Replacement laces for ArbPro Clip N Step boots
Also fit the ArbPro Evo
Keep boots snug on spurs and footholds
Cheap fix that extends boot life
Keep a spare pair in the gear bag
specs: ArbPro Clip N Step and Evo boots

p: Climbing boots take a beating from bark, spur straps and gaffs, and laces are usually the first thing to go. A frayed lace that snaps mid-climb leaves you with a loose boot on a spur, which costs control and can strain an ankle. Replacing laces at the first sign of fraying is cheap insurance.
Laces made for the boot fit the eyelets and hooks properly and come in the right length, so you are not left with long tails that catch on gear or brush.

Laces also wear where they cross spur straps and where they rub on hooks at the top of the boot. Check those spots when you put your boots on in the morning. A pair of replacement laces costs far less than a day lost to a broken lace on a climbing job, so it makes sense to change both boots at the same time.
Lace the boot snug through the instep and finish so the ends are tucked away from spur straps. Check laces and eyelets when you inspect your spurs and pads. More footwear is in arborist boots.
Boots are part of your safety kit: replace them when the soles, support or protection are worn out, not just the laces.

faq.q: Will these laces fit other boots?
faq.a: They are made for the ArbPro Clip N Step and Evo. They may fit other boots, but check length before relying on them.

faq.q: How often should I replace boot laces?
faq.a: Replace them as soon as you see fraying or cuts. Keeping a spare pair in the truck saves a day.

body.h: Choosing and using a throw weight
p: A throw weight carries the throw line up and over your chosen union, then drops back down the far side. Heavier bags carry farther and drop through foliage more easily; lighter bags are easier to control in a dense canopy and are less likely to hang up. Many climbers keep two weights so they can switch based on the tree.

Tie or clip the throw line to the weight's ring, flake the line into a cube or bag so it pays out cleanly, and use an underhand or two-handed throw for control. Once set, isolate the line to the union you want before pulling up rope.

Keep throw line and weights together in a cube or bag so they come out of the truck ready to use and free of knots. When a weight hangs up in the canopy, pull gently and try to shake it free rather than yanking hard, which can wedge it deeper or snap the line. A spare weight in the kit keeps the job moving if one stays in the tree.

Throw weights come down fast. Keep the drop zone clear, wear a helmet, and call out before each throw. Watch for power lines and never throw near conductors. Throw lines and kits are in throw weights and line.
Inspect the bag, ring and stitching regularly and retire a weight that is splitting.

faq.q: What weight should I start with?
faq.a: Many climbers start with a mid-weight bag and add a heavier one for tall trees. Choose based on throw height and canopy density.

faq.q: What throw line works with these weights?
faq.a: Any good arborist throw line that ties or clips securely to the ring. Thinner lines run more easily but tangle more if not flaked well.

name: Yale Polydyne Rigging Rope, 1/2 in

highlights: 1/2 in rigging rope from Yale Cordage
Easy to handle for light rigging
Works through common 1/2 in blocks
For limb lowering and small tops
Confirm rated strength on the rope's tag

p: Most crews carry rigging lines in more than one size. A 1/2 in line is the one you grab for pruning cuts, lowering limbs over a roof, and small top pieces. It is lighter to haul up and easier to run through a block or a natural crotch than a 5/8 or 3/4 bull rope, and it is kinder on the ground worker's hands.
It is not the rope for big wood. When piece size climbs, so do the dynamic forces, and you need a heavier line, block and sling to match.

On a typical pruning job a crew might use the 1/2 in line to lower limbs over a roof or garden while a heavier bull rope stays in the truck for the removal next door. Having both sizes on hand means the ground worker is not wrestling a heavy rope through small blocks when a lighter line would handle the work more easily and with better control.

Check the rated strength on Yale's tag and keep working loads well within it, allowing for shock loading. Inspect for cuts, glazing, flat spots and pulled strands before each job, and keep the rope clean and dry in a bag. Compare sizes in rigging rope.

Never use rigging rope for climbing. Rig within the rated strength of every component, inspect gear before each job, and make sure the crew is trained in rigging practice under ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions.

faq.q: Can I climb on Polydyne rigging rope?
faq.a: No. Use only rope rated and sold for life support as a climbing line.

faq.q: Is 1/2 in strong enough for tree removal?
faq.a: For limbs and small tops, often yes. Larger pieces need a larger rope and matched hardware. Check the rope's rated strength.

name: Bump Cap for Sena SMH10 Headset

Hands-free talk with climber and crew
Lighter than a full helmet for low-risk tasks
Protects against minor bumps only
Not a substitute for a rated helmet

p: Clear talk between the climber and ground crew makes rigging safer and faster. Hand signals and shouting over a saw or chipper both have limits. A Bluetooth headset like the SMH10 lets people talk hands-free, and a bump cap gives a light place to mount it for crew members who are away from the drop zone.
Check that the SMH10 parts and mounting fit the cap, and pair and test headsets before work starts.

Headsets earn their keep on jobs with loud machinery running. A ground worker feeding the chipper or running a lowering line can hear the climber's call without shutting anything down, and the climber can hear back that the line is ready. Agree on simple, standard commands and confirm each one so nothing is left to guesswork when the radio is open.

body.h: Know what a bump cap is for
p: A bump cap protects against minor knocks only. It is not a hard hat and is not rated for falling objects. Anyone in the work zone under a climber, near rigging or felling must wear an appropriately rated helmet per ANSI Z133 and site rules. Helmet-mounted systems are in communication.
Use communication gear as an addition to, not a replacement for, agreed crew commands.

faq.q: Can I wear this bump cap under a climber?
faq.a: No. Anyone in the drop zone or near rigging needs a rated helmet. A bump cap is for low-risk tasks only.

faq.q: Does it include the SMH10 headset?
faq.a: Check the listing. Typically the cap is sold for use with an SMH10 you already own.

body.h: How a 5/8 in lanyard works in the tree
p: A lanyard holds you in position while you cut, so you can lean back and free both hands. A 5/8 in line is thicker than most modern lanyards, which makes it easy to grab and gives a lot of material to wear before it needs replacing. Climbers who spend a lot of time on spurs on removals often like a heavier lanyard for its durability.
The trade-off is weight and how it works with adjusters and hitches. Make sure your adjuster or hitch cord is rated and suited to 5/8 in rope.

Static kernmantle construction gives very little stretch, so the lanyard holds you in position firmly without bouncing as you lean back. That firm feel is one reason some climbers prefer it for spur work on removals. Keep in mind that low stretch also means little shock absorption, so avoid slack in the lanyard and never put yourself in a position to fall onto it.

Check the cover for cuts, glazing and core shots, and inspect terminations and connectors every climb. A lanyard is never a cut-resistant device, so keep the saw away from it and consider a wire-core flipline for heavy saw work around the lanyard. Compare options in rope lanyards.
Life-support gear must meet the applicable standard, be used per the manufacturer's instructions and ANSI Z133, be inspected before every climb, and be used only by trained climbers.

faq.q: Is a 5/8 in lanyard too heavy?
faq.a: It is heavier than an 11 to 13mm lanyard, but some climbers prefer it for grip and durability, especially on removals.

faq.q: What adjuster works with 5/8 in rope?
faq.a: Use only an adjuster or hitch the manufacturer rates for that diameter. Check compatibility before you buy.

Before buying, check the current engine, deck size and drive details for the model year you are getting, and make sure parts and service are easy to get locally.

For tree companies, a reliable commercial mower can round out a grounds service offering without adding a lot of extra equipment. It fits on a trailer alongside the chipper, handles post-job cleanup of lawns and edges, and can work routes between tree jobs. Choose a mower with a deck and drive that suit the properties you actually maintain.

Read the operator's manual, keep guards and the discharge chute in place, and walk the area for sticks, stones and debris before mowing. Wear eye and hearing protection and sturdy boots. Other jobsite equipment is in power equipment.
Keep blades sharp and balanced, check oil and air filter before each day, and stick to the service intervals in the manual. Stop the engine and wait for the blade to stop before clearing the deck.

faq.q: Is the W520 battery powered?

name: Ring Slings for Tree Rigging
title: Ring Slings for Arborist Rigging: How to Choose

Ring accepts a block, pulley or lowering line
Quick to set and retrieve
Available in several rope sizes and lengths
Pair with a block and rigging line rated for the load

p: Wrap the sling around the stem, pass the eye through the ring and cinch it down. The choke grips the stem, so the sling holds its place on a vertical spar where a basket hitch would slip. Clip a block to the eye and you have a rigging point; tie the lowering line to the sling and you have a choker on the piece.
Pick a length that wraps the stems you usually work with and leaves room to choke, and a rope size matched to your block and the wood you are taking down.

Ring slings come in a wide range of sizes, from light 1/2 in versions for pruning and small tops to heavy slings for large removals. Many crews keep several lengths and sizes in the rigging bag, so they always have one that fits the stem and the load. Mark slings by size so the ground crew can grab the right one quickly.
Every component in the system needs to be rated for the dynamic forces involved, which can be several times the weight of the piece. Browse rigging slings to compare sizes and types.

Inspect the rope for cuts, glazing and stiff spots, and the ring for grooves, cracks and deformation. Rig within the rated strength of every component, inspect gear before each job, and make sure the crew is trained in rigging practice under ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions.

faq.q: What size ring sling should I buy?
faq.a: Match the rope diameter and rating to your rigging block and the size of wood you handle, and choose a length that wraps your typical stems.

faq.q: Can I use a ring sling as a friction saver for climbing?
faq.a: Only if it is rated and sold for life support. Rigging slings should not be used for climbing.

The Polycomb insert gives the cover a stiff top so it does not sag into the bucket and collect water. Measure your bucket's top opening before ordering to confirm the 28 x 34 in size.

The cover also helps keep tools, ropes and gear stored in the bucket dry and in better condition between jobs. On trucks parked outdoors overnight, a covered bucket means the operator starts the day without bailing out water or scraping wet leaves off the floor, and keeps the bucket liner cleaner for its regular inspections.
Remove the cover fully before operating the boom, and stow it so it cannot blow loose. Brush off debris and let it dry before long storage. More gear for aerial work is in bucket truck accessories.

body.h: Setting up a saddle that works for you
p: No two climbers set up a saddle the same way. Some want a handsaw on one hip and a top-handle saw on the other; some want every biner on a dedicated loop. Accessories such as extra gear loops, tool holders and storage clips let you put each piece of kit where your hand expects it, so you are not searching for it with a saw running.
Replacement bridges, leg loops and pads keep an older saddle in service, as long as the saddle maker allows those parts on that model.

Before adding anything, empty the saddle and look at how you actually work for a day. Note which tools you reach for most and where they get in the way. Then add accessories one at a time, so each change makes sense. Too many loops and holders can add weight and snag on branches, which works against the point of a tidy, efficient setup.

Use only parts the saddle maker approves for your model, especially for anything load-bearing such as bridges and attachment points. Never clip life-support connections to a gear loop. Compare full saddles in saddles and harnesses.
Life-support gear must meet the applicable standard, be used per the manufacturer's instructions and ANSI Z133, be inspected before every climb, and be used only by trained climbers.

faq.q: Can I use any bridge on my saddle?
faq.a: No. Use only bridges the saddle manufacturer approves for that model, installed as the manual describes.

faq.q: Are gear loops rated for life support?
faq.a: No. Gear loops are for tools and equipment only. Connect life-support gear to rated attachment points.

name: Clutch Drum Assembly for Husqvarna 550XP Mark II
title: Husqvarna 550XP Mark II Clutch Drum Assembly

Replace when the sprocket is grooved or worn
Helps new chain run true

body.h: When to replace the clutch drum
p: The sprocket on the clutch drum drives the chain, and it wears every time the saw cuts. A worn sprocket has grooves where the chain drive links sit and will chew up a new chain quickly. Many saw shops suggest replacing the sprocket every two chains or so, or whenever you see clear wear.
Also replace the drum if it is blued from heat, cracked, or wobbles on the crank, or if the needle bearing is worn.

A worn clutch drum can also make the saw feel rough or noisy at idle, and a damaged needle bearing can let the drum wobble and wear the chain unevenly. If the chain keeps turning at idle, look at the clutch springs and idle setting too. Inspect the drum whenever you change the chain, so problems are caught before they damage other parts.

Match the sprocket pitch to your bar and chain, and grease the needle bearing per Husqvarna's service information. Check the clutch shoes and springs while you are in there. More parts are in power equipment parts.
Make sure the saw is off and cool before working on it, and test the chain brake after reassembly.

faq.q: Do I need to change the chain at the same time?
faq.a: Running a new chain on a worn sprocket shortens its life, and an old chain can wear a new sprocket fast. Many crews replace them together.

faq.q: Will this fit the original 550XP?
faq.a: Confirm compatibility for your exact model and version before ordering.

name: Buckingham TreeSqueeze Friction Saver
title: Buckingham TreeSqueeze Friction Saver
meta: The Buckingham TreeSqueeze is a friction saver that protects the bark and your rope at the tie-in point. How it works, setup tips, inspection, and price.
tagline: A Buckingham friction saver for protecting the tree and your climbing line at the tie-in.
summary: The Buckingham TreeSqueeze is a friction saver from Buckingham, used at the tie-in point to protect the tree's bark and cut down wear on the climbing line. It gives a smoother, more predictable tie-in than running rope directly over a branch union.
highlights: Protects bark at the tie-in point
Reduces wear on your climbing line
Smoother, more predictable rope movement
From Buckingham, a long-time arborist gear maker
Retrievable from the ground with practice

p: Running a climbing line straight over a union generates heat, wears the rope, and damages the cambium. A friction saver puts a protective sleeve or connectors at the crotch so the rope runs on hardware instead of bark. The tree stays healthier and your rope lasts longer, and rope movement is smoother and easier to predict.
Set it high in a sound union with the rings or connectors positioned so they do not bind. Learn the retrieval method for your system on the ground before relying on it.

Friction savers also make it easier to repeat climbs in the same tree. Once the saver is set, the climber can come down, move ground gear and go back up on the same tie-in without fighting rope friction over bark. On trees with thin or sensitive bark, the protection it gives the cambium is worth the small extra time spent on setup.

A friction saver is part of your life-support system. Inspect the sleeve, rope or webbing and hardware before each climb and retire it at the first sign of cuts, heavy wear or heat damage. Compare other friction savers if you want an adjustable model.
Life-support gear must meet the applicable standard, be used per the manufacturer's instructions and ANSI Z133, be inspected before every climb, and be used only by trained climbers.

faq.q: Can I retrieve the TreeSqueeze from the ground?
faq.a: Many friction savers can be retrieved from the ground with the right setup. Follow Buckingham's instructions and practice low before using it aloft.

faq.q: Is a friction saver required?
faq.a: Not always, but it protects the tree and rope and is widely recommended for moving rope climbing.

Check what adjuster and connectors come in the kit, and make sure they suit your saddle setup and the way you clip in.

Lighter lanyards also tend to be more comfortable on long pruning days, when the climber moves around the canopy far more than on a straightforward removal. Less weight hanging on the side D-rings means less drag on the saddle and less fatigue by late afternoon. Make sure the lanyard length and connectors still suit the largest stems you plan to work around.

Inspect the rope, terminations, adjuster and carabiners before every climb. A lanyard is not cut-resistant; keep the saw well clear and consider a steel-core flipline for heavy saw work. More options are in lanyard kits.
Life-support gear must meet the applicable standard, be used per the manufacturer's instructions and ANSI Z133, be inspected before every climb, and be used only by trained climbers.

faq.q: Is the hipSTAR Flex Light a primary climbing system?

faq.q: How long should the lanyard be?

Many climbers keep a couple of ovals in their kit specifically for pulleys and rings and use D-shaped biners for the lanyard and bridge, where strength along the spine matters most. Keeping the oval in that role makes it easy to check, and makes sure its strength rating is well suited to the job you are asking of it each day.

Life-support gear must meet the applicable standard, be used per the manufacturer's instructions and ANSI Z133, be inspected before every climb, and be used only by trained climbers.

This bar is set up for 3/8 in mini pitch chain, the narrow-kerf Pixel style Husqvarna uses on many small saws, at .050 in gauge. Check your saw's manual for approved bar lengths and mounts, and match the drive link count to the bar length.
Small-kerf chain cuts fast with less power, which is why it suits compact and top-handle saws.

Small saws with narrow-kerf chain are popular for pruning because they cut quickly and are light to carry aloft. That same narrow kerf means the bar and chain wear faster if they are not kept sharp and well oiled. Check that the oiler is working and keep spare chains on hand, so the bar is never run with a dull or dry chain.

Flip the bar regularly so the rails wear evenly, clean out the groove and oil hole, and dress burrs off the rails with a file. Replace the bar if the rails are spread, the groove is worn shallow, or the nose is damaged. Other sizes are in chainsaw bars.
Keep the chain sharp and correctly tensioned and wear chainsaw protective gear, following the operator's manual and ANSI Z133.

faq.q: What length do I need?
faq.a: Check your saw's manual for approved bar lengths and order the matching chain length and drive link count.

name: ISC 1/2 in Rigging Block with Loopie Sling

meta: An ISC 1/2 in rigging block paired with a loopie sling for setting fast, adjustable rigging points on light to mid-size wood. How it rigs, checks, and price.
tagline: An ISC rigging block for 1/2 in rope, paired with an adjustable loopie sling.
summary: This ISC 1/2 in rigging block with loopie sling is a ready-to-go rigging kit for light to mid-size wood. The loopie cinches to the stem and the block gives you a clean, low-friction redirect for your lowering line.
highlights: ISC rigging block for 1/2 in rope
Adjustable loopie sling included
Side plates open to load the rope mid-line
For limb lowering and small tops
Check ratings on the block and sling

body.h: Setting a rigging point with block and loopie
p: A block above the work lets you lower pieces with the rope running over a sheave instead of rubbing over bark. The loopie is an adjustable sling that cinches tight to the stem, so it fits a range of diameters and holds its place. Together they make a rigging point you can set in a minute and retrieve easily.
A 1/2 in kit is aimed at limbs and small tops. For bigger pieces, move up to a larger block, rope and sling rated for the forces involved.

Kits like this save time on the job because all the parts are matched and ready to go. The block and sling stay together in the bag, so the climber can grab one kit and know everything inside suits the same rope size. Keep a spare set of carabiners or shackles with it that match the block's rating, so nothing gets mixed up.

Check the working load limit and MBS on the block and sling, and match the rigging line and connectors. Rigging loads can be several times the piece's weight once it starts moving. Other kits are in rigging kits.

Inspect the sheave, bearing, side plates and sling before each job. Rig within the rated strength of every component, inspect gear before each job, and make sure the crew is trained in rigging practice under ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions.

faq.q: Can I use 5/8 in rope in this block?
faq.a: Use only the rope sizes ISC lists for the block. This kit is sized for 1/2 in rope.

faq.q: Is the loopie adjustable?
faq.a: Yes. A loopie cinches and adjusts to fit different stem sizes.

name: Stump Grinder Bolts
title: Stump Grinder Bolts: Replacement Tooth Bolts
meta: Replacement stump grinder bolts for holding teeth and pockets on the cutter wheel. Why fresh bolts matter, how to match them to your wheel, and typical price.
tagline: Replacement bolts for securing teeth and pockets on a stump grinder cutter wheel.
summary: Stump grinder bolts hold the teeth and pockets on the cutter wheel, and they take a beating every time the wheel hits a stump. Replacing worn or stretched bolts when you change teeth keeps the wheel safe and the teeth tight.
highlights: Replacement bolts for cutter wheel teeth
Fresh bolts help teeth stay tight
Match thread and length to your wheel
Replace stretched or damaged bolts
Keep spares with the tooth kit
specs: Match to your cutter wheel and tooth system
Torque to the wheel maker's specification

p: A stump grinder wheel turns fast and slams into wood, soil and rock. Bolts holding teeth and pockets stretch, rust and lose clamp force over time. A loose tooth can wear the wheel, throw debris or break off. Many operators replace bolts every time they change teeth, or at least whenever a bolt shows any wear or thread damage.
Match the bolt to your tooth and pocket system by thread size, length and head style. Check the wheel or tooth maker's specifications rather than guessing.

Also check the cutter wheel itself while teeth and bolts are off. Look for cracks around the pockets, worn or elongated bolt holes, and damage to the wheel edge. A wheel with worn holes will not hold bolts at the right torque, no matter how new they are, so it needs repair or replacement before going back into service.
Torque bolts to the wheel manufacturer's specification and recheck after the first stump. Use new nuts or lock washers as specified. More stump grinding gear is in stump grinding.
Shut down the machine and lock out the wheel before working on it, and wear eye protection and gloves. Keep bystanders well clear when grinding.

faq.q: Do I need new bolts with new teeth?
faq.a: Many operators replace them together. At minimum, replace any bolt that is stretched, bent, rusted or has thread damage.

faq.q: How do I know which bolt fits?
faq.a: Match the bolt to your tooth and pocket system's thread, length and head style. Check the maker's specifications.

name: Yale R.I.N.G. ART Positioner Lanyard Kit

meta: The Yale R.I.N.G. ART Positioner lanyard kit pairs Yale rope with the ART Positioner adjuster for fast, smooth length changes. Setup, inspection, and price.

summary: The Yale R.I.N.G. ART Positioner lanyard kit pairs a Yale Cordage lanyard with the ART Positioner mechanical adjuster, giving one-handed length changes while you work. It is a popular setup for climbers who reposition constantly on removals and big pruning jobs.
highlights: Yale lanyard rope with an ART Positioner adjuster
One-handed lanyard adjustment
Smooth tending in both directions
Built for constant repositioning
Inspect rope, adjuster and connectors every climb

p: The ART Positioner is a mechanical lanyard adjuster that lets you shorten and lengthen your lanyard smoothly with one hand. Compared with a friction hitch on the lanyard, it tends more cleanly and adjusts without needing to break a hitch loose. Pairing it with a Yale rope chosen for the device gives a kit that works out of the box.
Set it up per the ART instructions and practice adjusting on the ground before using it in the tree.

Climbers who move around a lot during pruning work often find a mechanical adjuster speeds up every reposition, since a quick pull or release changes the lanyard length without stopping to dress a hitch. On removals it lets you tighten up firmly into a cut and then let out slack to move down the stem without unclipping from the tree.

Inspect the rope, terminations, Positioner cam and spring, and carabiners before every climb. Replace worn rope and parts as the manuals direct. A lanyard is not cut-resistant, so keep saws clear. Compare other lanyard kits.
Life-support gear must meet the applicable standard, be used per the manufacturer's instructions and ANSI Z133, be inspected before every climb, and be used only by trained climbers.

faq.q: Can I put the Positioner on a different rope later?
faq.a: Only on rope types and diameters ART approves for the Positioner. Check the instructions before swapping.

faq.q: Is the kit ready to climb on?
faq.a: Assemble and inspect it per the instructions, and test it near the ground before using it aloft.

name: Husqvarna Oil Pump Assembly for 562XP Chainsaw
title: Husqvarna 562XP Oil Pump Assembly
h1: Husqvarna Oil Pump Assembly for 562XP Chainsaw
meta: Replacement Husqvarna oil pump assembly for the 562XP chainsaw. Signs the pump is failing, what to check first, how to confirm fit, and typical price.
tagline: A replacement chain oil pump for the Husqvarna 562XP.
summary: This Husqvarna 562XP oil pump assembly is the replacement pump that feeds bar and chain oil to the bar. If the bar is running dry even with a clean bar oil hole and a full tank, the pump is the next thing to check.
highlights: Replacement oil pump for the Husqvarna 562XP
Restores bar and chain lubrication
Prevents bar and chain damage from running dry
Confirm fit by model and serial
Check the oil filter and lines first

p: A saw that throws no oil off the chain will cook a bar and chain fast. Before replacing the pump, clean the oil hole on the bar and the bar mount, check the tank pickup filter, and look for a cracked or pinched oil line. If those are good and the saw still runs dry, the pump or its drive is likely worn.
Hold the running saw over a light surface and rev it; a healthy pump throws a visible line of oil within a few seconds.

Running a saw without proper oiling quickly heats the bar, stretches the chain and wears the sprocket and bar rails. Even a short stretch of cutting with no oil can do real damage. Replacing the pump early, once oiling becomes weak or uneven, is much cheaper than replacing a scorched bar and chain along with it.
Follow Husqvarna's service information, check the pump drive gear or worm on the crank side, and set any adjustable flow screw to suit your bar length. More parts are in power equipment parts.
Work on a cool saw with the spark plug lead off, and test the chain brake and oiling before cutting.

faq.q: Will the 562XP pump fit the 565 or 572XP?
faq.a: Do not assume it will. Confirm compatibility for your exact model before ordering.

faq.q: Can I adjust oil flow?
faq.a: Many Husqvarna pro saws have an adjustable pump. Check the manual for your model.

name: Yale Guardian Bracing System
title: Yale Guardian Bracing System for Tree Support
meta: The Yale Guardian bracing system is a synthetic tree support system for limbs and codominant stems. How synthetic support works, install notes, and price.
tagline: A synthetic support system from Yale Cordage for limbs and codominant stems.
summary: The Yale Guardian bracing system is a synthetic tree support system from Yale Cordage for supplemental support of codominant stems and heavy limbs. It is a lighter, quicker install than traditional steel cable for many jobs.
highlights: Synthetic supplemental tree support
From Yale Cordage
Lighter and quicker to install than steel
Allows some natural movement
Schedule regular inspections after install
specs: Supplemental support of limbs and stems

p: Synthetic systems are installed high in the crown between stems to limit how far a weak union or heavy limb can move. Many wrap the stems rather than relying on drilled hardware, are light enough to carry aloft in one trip, and let the tree move naturally in the wind instead of holding it rigid.
Deciding whether and where to support a tree is an arborist assessment. Follow Yale's instructions and ANSI A300 guidance for system selection and placement.

Synthetic systems are also popular because they reduce the need for drilling, which some clients and arborists prefer to avoid on valuable trees. Lighter components are easy to carry and install aloft, and adjustments can be made in place. Keep records of each install, including date, location and tension, so future inspections can track how the system and tree are performing.

Size the system to the stems involved and set it at the tension the manufacturer specifies. Inspect it on a regular schedule and after big storms for abrasion, UV damage, slippage and bark growth around the system. Related cordage is in rigging rope.
Supplemental support reduces risk but does not eliminate it. Work aloft only with trained crew under ANSI Z133.

faq.q: Is synthetic bracing as strong as steel cable?
faq.a: Systems are rated differently. Choose a system rated for the stems you are supporting and follow the manufacturer's sizing guidance.

faq.q: How long does synthetic support last?
faq.a: Service life depends on the product, exposure and conditions. Follow Yale's guidance and inspect regularly.
